caseno: Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989 and Writ Petition No. 920 of 1989.
lawyer:
TH Khan with Shah Md. Habibur Rahman, Advocate ----- For Petitioners in both the Writ Petitions 
Md. Saidur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For Respondent No.1. 
Ziaur Rahman Khan, Advocate ----- For Respondent No.4.
parties:
MA Salam alias Abdus Salam ------ Petitioner
[In Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989]
Obaidullah alias Md. Obaidullah and others ------ Petitioners
[In Write Petition No. 920 of 1989]
vs
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: On an application being Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989 filed at the instance of MA Salam alias Abdus Salam on 6.8.89 and another being Writ Petition No. 920 of 1989 filed at the instance of Obaidullah alias Md. Obaidullah and others on 26.10.1989 Rule Nisi were issued by this court calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 11.3.1989 passed by the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka in the land acquisition proceedings namely, LA Case No. 9 of 1988 making his decision final under section 5(1) of Ordinance II of 1982 regarding acquisition of the proceeding lands belonging to the petitioner contained in Annexures-'F' and 'E' respectively should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989 and the petitioners in Writ Petition 920 of 1989 claim to be the co-sharer and owner of the land measuring 0.0975 acres. It is stated in their respective petitions that the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989 along with one Abdul Hannan the petitioner Nos. 1-3 and the petitioner No. 4 Atar Banu of Writ Petition No. 920 of 1989 became owners of the land measuring 0.0975 acres equivalent to more or less 6 kathas of land of Plot. Nos. 119 and 120 and 253 appertaining to CS Khatian 84 of Mouza Tejturi Bazar JL No. 264 PS Tejgaon, District-Dhaka which was said to have been acquired under order dated 11.3.1989 passed by the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka in LA Case No.9 of 1988-89 contained in Annexure-'F' of Writ Petition No. 863 of 1989 and Annexure-'E' of Writ Petition No. 920 of 1989. 

 5. The land of the petitioners measuring 0.0975 purported to have been acquired under the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 for the so- called public purpose or in the public interest for widening of the Tejgoan Airport Road (Old) in its turning towards west just near the southern side of the over bridge at Farmgate. The proceeding land is on the western side of the Airport Road, intervened by the footpath of the Airport Road. On its southern side lies Firm View (Super Market), on its northern side lies the starting paint of the Indira Road. On the eastern side runs the Airport (Old) Highway and on its contiguous west lies the four storied Chowrangee Super Market. The proceeding land stands on the plot Nos.119 and 120 and 253 and is covered by the Municipal holding Nos. 99, 100, 101/1 and 104. The petitioners previously had four storied building on the said plot in 1974. The respondent No. 4 RAJUK published a notification in the daily "Inqilab" dated 16.3.1987 directing the owners of the building on the two sides of the Airport road to beautify their front sides facing the road with a direction to submit plan for approval failing which there would be no alternative but to acquire the property for doing the necessary beautification works. Thereafter on the direction of the respondent No. 4, the entire front side of the building was demolished in part and the building Inspector submitted his report before the Chairman RAJUK to that effect. The respondent No. 4 not being satisfied with the part demolition thereafter demolished the entire 4 storied commercial building by bulldozer in August 1988 causing heavy loss to the petitioners. While the petitioners were trying to get the plan for construction of the building approved LA Case No. 9 of 1988-89 was initiated on 20.1.89 by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka for the purpose of permanent acquisition of land measuring 0.0975 acres equivalent to 6 Imams of the CS Plot Nos. 119,120 and 253 belonging to the petitioners. LA Case No. 9 of 1988-89 was initiated on the direction of Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Respondent No. 1. The respondents acted malafide in initiating the proceeding of LA Case No. 9 of 1988-89 inasmuch as the widening of the turning of the Airport Road is neither feasible nor practicable because of the over bridge standing just towards the north of the proceeding land and south of the Indira Road. It is submitted that as the notice under sections 3, 4 and 6 were not issued to the petitioners they were not aware about the initiation of the proceeding of LA Case No.9 of 1988-89 till the 3rd week of April 1989 when for the first time the notice under section 7 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Property Ordinance 1982 was served upon the petitioners. It is also submitted that the purported requisition and acquisition of the property of the petitioner is not for public purpose inasmuch as it has not been practicable to utilize the land for the purpose for which it has been acquired and the land has still been kept vacant. 

 6. Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 having filed affidavit-in-opposition are represented by the Assistant Attorney-General Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman and Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan, the learned Counsel has appeared for the respondent No. 4 RAJUK on whose behalf separate affidavit-in-opposition has been filed. All the respondents opposed the Rule stating, inter alia, that the petitioners have not been able to prove their title by producing the title deeds in respect of the proceeding land along with the writ petitions. It is submitted that the land has been acquired after complying with the provisions laid down under sections 3, 4, 5 and 6 and other relevant provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance (Ordinance No. II of 1982) and the acquisition is for public purpose and has been made in public interest. It is also submitted that the compensation money having been determined by the Deputy Commissioner after consideration of the market value of the land in the vicinity as per section 6 of the Ordinance II of 1982, the requiring body has deposited the money to the authority and some portion of the compensation money has also been withdrawn by some of the co-sharers. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 4 it is asserted that on receipt of the notice the demolition of construction for beautification purpose the petitioners themselves removed the unauthorized construction raised by them on the land. It is submitted that the land measuring 0.0975 acres has been acquired initiating the proceeding through the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka for the purpose of widening and developing the turning point of the Airport Road near the overhead bridge at Farmgate. As per order of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, RAJUK has already placed an amount of Taka 29,17,185.97 by way of compensation for the land and the structures which has fallen within the acquisition scheme and subsequent to the deposit of compensation money the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka handed over possession of the land to RAJUK on 17.4.1989. After taking over possession development work will be started by RAJUK as per approved plan. 

 8. Mr. TH Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in both the Rules, has taken us through the application and the annexures thereof, the affidavit, supplementary affidavit and affidavits-in-opposition filed by both the parties. Besides alleging non-service of notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property(Ordinance No. II of 1982) the learned Advocate questioned the very enactment so far it relates to the mode and manner of service of notice of acquisition as prescribed under section 3 of the Ordinance. It is submitted that the provision of service of notice under section 3 of the Ordinance II of 1982 is violative of the provisions of Articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Ordinance No. II of 1982 has imposed unreasonable restriction over the right of the citizen but the provision of the Ordinance does not contemplate the service of notice personally on owner or the occupier of the proceeding land. Mr. TH Khan proceeded with his submission that the provision of requisition of Immovable Property Act, 1948 and those of the Land Acquisition Act, 1994, since repealed, stood the test of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution but the present legislation being Ordinance No. II of 1982 having not been placed in harmonious position with those of the repealed Acts, the enactment has been made in violation of the right guaranteed under the Constitution and for that matter this court in its writ jurisdiction is entitled to and should examine the question of reasonableness of the provision regarding the mode and manner of publication of notices under sections 3, 6, 7 particularly the provision of the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance which has offended the provision of Articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution. Article 31 of the Constitution of Bangladesh provides that "to enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law." 

 (2) A law made under clause (1) shall provide for the acquisition, nationalization or requisition with compensation and shall either fix the amount of compensation or specify the principles on which and the manner in which, the compensation is to be assessed and paid, but no such law shall be called in question in any court on the ground that any provision in respect of such compensation is not adequate. 

 (3) Nothing in this Article shall affect the operation of any law made before the commencement of the Proclamations (Amendment) Order, 1977 (Proclamations Order No. 1 of 1977), insofar as it relates to the acquisition, nationalization or acquisition of any property without compensation." 

 9. From the reading of the provision of Article 42(1)(2)(3) it appears that every citizen shall have right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalized or requisitioned save by the authority of law. Thus it is clear that though the citizens have an alienable right to acquire and hold and enjoy property, restriction has been imposed providing that the Government has the power to acquire and requisition the property by the authority of law on payment of compensation to be assessed by the authority and such acquisition and requisition cannot be called in question under sub-article (2) of Article 42 of the Constitution. The learned Advocate for the petitioner candidly admitted that there is no bar under the Constitution to make and promulgate such law for the acquisition and requisition of the property for the public purpose but the main grievance of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is against the mode, method and manner of service of notice as provided under section 3 of the Ordinance. The learned Advocate submitted that the provision of issuing and serving notice under section 3 of the Ordinance offends the public purpose inasmuch as the mode, manner and method of issuance of service under the Ordinance 1982 is different from the manner of serving and issuing notice as provided under the previous Act 1948 which was more rational. From the averments made and grounds taken in the petition it is found that the Rule was neither sought for nor issued challenging the procedure laid down under the Ordinance 1982 and in that view of the matter we do not consider it appropriate at this stage to assume the jurisdiction going to the extent of declaring the law itself as violative of the Constitution. Mr. TH Khan, the learned Advocate, then turned to the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance and submitted that the notice having not been served on the petitioners they were absolutely in dark about the proceeding and for that matter were unable to file objection against the proposed acquisition in due time. Section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 provides as follows: 

 "3. Publication of Preliminary Notice of acquisition of property: 

 10. From the perusal of the notice itself and the report submitted it appears that the notice under section 3 was served on the proceeding land and other places and, therefore, the petitioners cannot have grievance for not serving the notice personally on the petitioners claiming ownership of the proceeding land. The learned Advocate then argued that the notice under sections 3 and 6 do not contain the khatian number of the land sought to be acquired with proper specification and boundaries so as to enable the petitioners to raise objection. Mr. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General in reply submitted that the notice under sections 3 and 6 contained the plot number and the area of land measuring 0.0975 within mouza Testuribazar and the petitioners themselves having claimed that they had building over the land sought to be acquired we are of the view that the notice does not suffer from insufficiency and vagueness. From the statement made by the petitioners that they had a building which is alleged to have been demolished it appears that the petitioners were quite aware about the land sought to be acquired. Furthermore, this ground was not taken in the petition at the time of obtaining the Rule. For the aforesaid reasons we do not find substance in the above submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Mr. TH Khan then argued that the power conferred to the authority to requisition property necessarily postulates a definite, specified and identifiable property but in the instant case the order of requisition purported to requisition a vague, indefinite and unidentifiable part of the petitioners land and hence it cannot be sustained. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied on the case of Momtaz Begum vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 14 DLR 608 wherein it was observed: 

 11. The principle laid down in the case under reference is not applicable in the present case inasmuch as the decided case arose out of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act (XIII of 1948) the provision of which was different from the present case which has arisen out of an acquisition order under Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982). Over and above in the present case there was no difficulty for the petitioners to know about the area of land sought to be acquired so as to file objection against the proceeding earlier before the appropriate authority. 

 14. In the present case though in the notice issued under section 3 of the Ordinance, 1982 the land sought be acquired has not been delineated with specific boundaries but it has been described as part of three plots and it was clearly known to the petitioners as to which land was sought to be acquired. In order to substantiate his argument the learned Advocate referred to the case of Aminuddin Ahmed Chowdhury vs. Land Acquisition Collector and, others reported in 15 DLR 51 wherein it is held: 

 "As order of acquisition under section 3 could be justified if it had confined itself to the acres of land for which there was a necessity for immediate possession, but when such an order covers an amount of land which includes land which may be needed in future but for which there was no immediate necessity. The order even in respect of the area for which there was immediate necessity is illegal because the order operates as a whole." 

 15. The aforesaid case also rose out of acquisition and requisition of property under the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. The facts and circumstances of the said case is not similar to the facts of the present case where 0.0975 acres has been acquired under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 for the purpose of widening the turning of the Airport Road at the Farmgate and it cannot be said specifically at this stage as to how much land immediately will be necessary for the purpose. The learned Advocate also submits that the two alternative expression in the order that the land" is required" and "might be required "indicate the lack of application of mind and, as such, the order/notice for requisition is liable to be struck down on this ground also. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has cited the case of Sankar Gopal Chatterjee and ors vs. Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and ors reported in 41 DLR 326. We not find any force in the argument of the learned Advocate as we find from the perusal of the notice that though the words "is required" or "might be required" have been used but as a matter of fact there is no ambiguity over the same affording an opportunity to the petitioners to find fault in the notice of acquisition. The petitioners have also taken the ground in the petitions that having regard to the provision of section 8 of the Ordinance, 1982 along with section 1 sub-sections (a),(b),(c),(d),(e) and (f) of section 2 of the Ordinance the Deputy Commissioner is under obligation to determine the market value of the concerned land measuring 0.0975 which having not been done the compensation assessed is arbitrary and hence it is not acceptable to the petitioners. This ground relates to the compensation for which separate forum was open for the petitioners and hence this cannot be a ground for setting aside the order of acquisition of land, if it is otherwise found to have been validly made. Besides the grounds aruged above, Mr. Khan has drawn our attention to the fact that 0.0975 acres land was sought to be acquired for the purpose of the widening the turning of the Airport Road which is neither possible nor practicable because of the existing overhead bridge standing to the north of the Supermarket. It is further submitted that for the purpose of widening the turning of the Airport Road entire land would not be necessary and hence the order for acquiring land more than the actual requirement is malafide and, therefore, required to he declared as has been made without lawful authority and hence of no legal effect. Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General in reply submitted that the land has been acquired for widening the turning of the Airport Road is a public purpose and whether the total land will be necessary or not could only be seen at the time of execution of the work. It is submitted that though the acquisition proceeding is complete and on the deposit of compensation money by the requiring body RAJUK the land has been handed over to them but the work could not be started because of the stay order obtained from this court It is also submitted by Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 that after the completion of the work of widening of the road it could be ascertained by the RAJUK whether the entire land will be necessary and if any portion be found to have remained surplus could be utilized for any other public purpose or could be returned to the owners. This could be ascertained by the authority only after the execution of work. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan has also argued that there being disputed question of fact in respect of the claim of title over the land sought to be acquired the relief sought for is beyond the scope of writ jurisdiction of this court. It is also argued that the petitioners who have moved this writ application being not the aggrieved persons are not entitled to move this application against the impugned acquisition proceeding. As the rise and the fall of the petitioners depend on the legality or otherwise of the process of acquisition taken under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) we restrain ourselves from entering into the question of title of the petitioners in respect of the proceeding land. Having conceded that the widening of a road is a public purpose Mr. TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has finally argued that keeping of the land which is actually required for the purpose of widening of the turning the Airport Road, the remaining portion can be and should be returned to the petitioners and in support of his submission the learned Advocate has referred to the unreported case being Writ Petition No. 72 of 1988 wherein it is held that: 

 "The Government can withdraw from acquisition any property acquired under section 5 by notification published in the official Gazette, the Government can also withdraw from acquisition any property when taking of decision under section 5(6) in the matter is pending before it." 

 16. In the present case the land has been acquired under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982). There is no corresponding provision for withdrawal from acquisition when the process of acquisition has reached to its final stage. As the land has been acquired for the purpose of widening of the turning point of the Airport Road which is a public purpose it could only be ascertained after the execution of the work as to how much land will be actually necessary for the purpose. We do not find any infirmity in the order of acquisition of the land. If, however, any land out of the land acquired is found to have remained excess of the requirement after the execution of the work, it will be left open for the Government to decide as to whether the requiring body will be entitled to use the same for any public purpose other than the purpose for which it has been acquired and or is liable to return the same to the original owner after proper verification and scrutiny. 

 17. For the reasons stated above, we are of the view that the petitioners have not been successful in making out any convincing ground which calls for our interference by way of declaring that the impugned order of the acquisition of the land in question is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
